Viññattuttari abhihaṭṭhuṃ, ubhinnaṃ dūtakena ca.

The training rules on: acting as a go-between; on building a hut; on a monastery; on washing an old robe; on accepting a robe; on soliciting from an unrelated person; on accepting more than that; the two rules on what has been prepared; and on accepting a robe procured by a messenger.

Kosiyā suddhadvebhāgā, chabbassāni nisīdanaṃ;

Riñcanti rūpikā ceva, ubho nānappakārakā.

The training rule on a silk mixture; the training rules on pure black wool and on two parts; the training rule on six years; the training rule on a felt sitting-cloth; the training rule on having sheep's wool washed; the training rule on accepting gold and silver; and the two rules on transactions involving gold and silver and on various kinds of trade.

Ūnabandhanavassikā, suttaṃ vikappanena ca;

Dvāradānasibbāni [T 0.0227] dvāradānasibbinī (sī. syā.) ca, pūvapaccayajoti ca.

The training rules on: a bed with legs of less than five hand-spans and on a rains-cloth; on soliciting thread; concerning weavers; on a large monastery, on giving a robe, and on sewing a robe; and the rules concerning cakes (Kāṇamātā), requisites (Mahānāma), and kindling a fire.

Ratanaṃ sūci mañco ca, tūlaṃ nisīdanakaṇḍu ca;

Vassikā ca sugatena, viññatti aññaṃ cetāpanā.

The training rules on: jewels; a needle-case; a bed or bench; being stuffed with cotton; a sitting-cloth; a cloth for covering itches; a rains-cloth; the dimension of a robe; another kind of soliciting; and another kind of purchase.

Dve saṅghikā mahājanikā, dve puggalalahukā garu;

Dve vighāsā sāṭikā ca, samaṇacīvarena ca.

The two training rules on what is communal (one on what is intended for another, one on soliciting); the two training rules on what is for the general public (one on the item itself, one on soliciting); the training rule on soliciting what is for an individual; the training rule on a light robe; the training rule on a heavy robe; the two training rules on eating leftovers (first and second); the training rule on a bathing-cloth; and the training rule on giving a monk's robe.

Samapaññāsime dhammā, chahi ṭhānehi jāyare;

Kāyato na vācācittā, vācato na kāyamanā.

These fifty training rules arise from six origins. They arise from the body, not from speech and mind; they arise from speech, not from body and mind.

Kāyavācā na ca cittā na cittato (sī. syā.), kāyacittā na vācikā na vācato (sī. syā.);

Vācācittā [P 5.0088] na kāyena, tīhi dvārehi tīhi ṭhānehi (syā.) jāyare.

They arise from body and speech, not from mind; from body and mind, not from speech; from speech and mind, not from body; and from the three doors.

Chasamuṭṭhānikā ete, sañcarittena sādisā.

These have six origins; they are similar to the Sañcaritta training rule.

Sañcarittasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Here ends the section on the Sañcaritta Origin.

4. Samanubhāsanāsamuṭṭhānaṃ

4. The Samanubhāsanā Origin

261.

261.

Bhedānuvattadubbaca[M 0.0160][V 0.0182], dūsaduṭṭhulladiṭṭhi ca;

Chandaṃ ujjagghikā dve ca, dve ca saddā na byāhare.

The training rules on: following a schismatic, being difficult to admonish, corrupting families, concealing a gross offense, and not relinquishing a wrong view; on leaving without giving consent; the two on laughing loudly; the two on making little sound; and on not speaking.

Chamā nīcāsane ṭhānaṃ, pacchato uppathena ca;

Vajjānuvattigahaṇā, osāre paccācikkhanā.

The training rules on: sitting on the ground, sitting on a low seat, sitting while another is standing, walking behind, and walking off the path; on concealing a fault, following one who has been suspended, and the eight grounds for censure; on reinstating one who has been suspended; and the first rule on being angry.

Kismiṃ saṃsaṭṭhā dve vadhi, visibbe dukkhitāya ca;

Puna saṃsaṭṭhā na vūpasame, ārāmañca pavāraṇā.

The training rules on: 'in some case or other'; the two on being associated; on striking and making someone cry; on unsewing a robe; on an afflicted co-resident; again, on being associated; on not settling a matter; on a monastery; and on not inviting.

Anvaddhaṃ anvaddhamāsaṃ (sī. syā.) saha jīviniṃ, dve cīvaraṃ anubandhanā;

Sattatiṃsa [T 0.0228] ime dhammā, kāyavācāya cittato.

The training rules on: every half-month; the two on a co-resident; on a robe; and on pursuing. These thirty-seven rules arise from body, speech, and mind.

Sabbe ekasamuṭṭhānā, samanubhāsanā yathā.

All have a single origin, just as the rule on formal admonition.

Samanubhāsanāsamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Here ends the section on the Samanubhāsanā Origin.

5. Kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ

5. The Kathina Origin

262.

262.

Ubbhataṃ kathinaṃ tīṇi, paṭhamaṃ pattabhesajjaṃ;

Accekaṃ cāpi sāsaṅkaṃ, pakkamantena vā duve.

The three training rules on the Kathina being withdrawn; the first rule on a bowl and the rule on medicine; also the rule on an urgent robe-cloth; the rule on a dangerous place; and the two rules on departing.

Upassayaṃ paramparā, anatirittaṃ nimantanā;

Vikappaṃ rañño vikāle, vosāsāraññakena ca.

The training rules on: a bhikkhunī's quarters, eating consecutively, not leaving a remainder, an invitation, assigning, the royal inner quarters, entering a village at the wrong time; and the second and fourth rules to be acknowledged.

Ussayāsannicayañca, pure pacchā vikāle ca;

Pañcāhikā saṅkamanī, dvepi āvasathena ca.

The training rules on: speaking contentiously and accumulating bowls; on before the meal, after the meal, and at the wrong time; on five days; on transferring a robe; and also the two on a public rest house.

Pasākhe [V 0.0183] āsane ceva, tiṃsa ekūnakā ime;

Kāyavācā na ca cittā na cittato (syā.), tīhi dvārehi jāyare.

The training rules on a branch and on sitting on a seat. These twenty-nine rules arise from body and speech, and not from mind; they arise from the three doors.

Dvisamuṭṭhānikā sabbe, kathinena sahāsamā.

All are of dual origination, the same as the Kathina rule.

Kathinasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on the Origination of the Kathina is concluded.

6. Eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānaṃ

6. 6. The Chapter on the Origination of Goat's Hair

263.

263.

Eḷakalomā [M 0.0161] dve seyyā, āhacca piṇḍabhojanaṃ;

Gaṇavikālasannidhi, dantaponena celakā.

The training rules on: goat's hair; the two on lying down together; on having a removable foot and on alms-food from a public rest house; on eating in a group, eating at the wrong time, and storing up; on a tooth-stick; and on a naked ascetic.

Uyyuttaṃ senaṃ uyyuttaṃ vase (syā.) uyyodhi, surā orena nhāyanā;

Dubbaṇṇe dve desanikā, lasuṇupatiṭṭhe naccanā.

The training rules on: a deployed army, an army residence, and a mock battle; on drinking intoxicants; on bathing within half a month; on making a discolored mark; the first and third rules to be acknowledged; on garlic; on attending; and on a festival on a mountain top.

Nhānamattharaṇaṃ seyyā, antoraṭṭhe tathā bahi;

Antovassaṃ [T 0.0229] cittāgāraṃ, āsandi suttakantanā.

The training rules on: being naked; the second on deportment; the first on deportment; on within the kingdom and likewise outside the kingdom; on within the rains-retreat; on a painted chamber; on a long-legged chair; and on spinning thread.

Veyyāvaccaṃ sahatthā ca, abhikkhukāvāsena ca;

Chattaṃ yānañca saṅghāṇiṃ, alaṅkāraṃ gandhavāsitaṃ.

The training rules on: performing a service for a householder; on giving with one's own hand; on a residence without a bhikkhu; on an umbrella and footwear; on a vehicle; on a waist-cloth; on a woman's adornment, on scented cosmetics, and on scented oil-cake.

Bhikkhunī sikkhamānā ca, sāmaṇerī gihiniyā;

Asaṃkaccikā āpatti, cattārīsā catuttari.

The training rules on: rubbing a bhikkhunī, rubbing a female probationer, rubbing a female novice, and rubbing a laywoman; and the offense of not wearing a breast-cloth. These are forty-four rules.

Kāyena na vācācittena, kāyacittena na vācato;

Dvisamuṭṭhānikā sabbe, samā eḷakalomikāti.

They arise from the body, not from speech and mind; they arise from body and mind, not from speech. All are of dual origination, the same as the rule on goat's hair.

Eḷakalomasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on the Origination of Goat's Hair is concluded.

7. Padasodhammasamuṭṭhānaṃ

7. 7. The Chapter on the Origination of Word-by-Word Dhamma

264.

264.

Padaññatra [V 0.0184] asammatā, tathā atthaṅgatena ca;

Tiracchānavijjā [P 5.0089] dve vuttā, anokāso anokāse (sī. syā.) ca pucchanā.

The training rules on: word-by-word Dhamma, teaching Dhamma, and giving an exhortation; likewise, on after sunset; the two declared rules on worldly arts; and on asking a question without having been given leave.

Satta sikkhāpadā ete, vācā na kāyacittato kāyacittakā (ka.);

Vācācittena jāyanti, na tu kāyena jāyare.

These seven training rules arise from speech, not from body and mind. They arise from speech and mind, but do not arise from the body.

Dvisamuṭṭhānikā sabbe, padasodhammasadisā.

All are of dual origination, similar to the rule on word-by-word Dhamma.

Padasodhammasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on the Origination of Word-by-Word Dhamma is concluded.

8. Addhānasamuṭṭhānaṃ

8. 8. The Chapter on the Origination of a Journey

265.

265.

Addhānanāvaṃ [M 0.0162] paṇītaṃ, mātugāmena saṃhare;

Dhaññaṃ nimantitā ceva, aṭṭha ca pāṭidesanī.

The training rule on arranging with a bhikkhunī for a journey, the training rule on embarking on a boat, the training rule on choice food, the training rule on arranging with a woman, the training rule on having hair removed, the training rule on raw grain, the training rule on eating elsewhere when invited, and the eight Pāṭidesanīya rules for bhikkhunīs.

Sikkhā pannarasa ete, kāyā na vācā na manā;

Kāyavācāhi jāyanti, na te cittena jāyare.

These fifteen training rules arise from the body, not from speech, not from mind; they arise from body and speech, but do not arise from mind.

Kāyacittena jāyanti, na te jāyanti vācato;

Kāyavācāhi cittena, samuṭṭhānā catubbidhā.

They arise from body and mind, but not from speech; and from body, speech, and mind. The origins are fourfold.

Paññattā [T 0.0230] buddhañāṇena, addhānena sahā samā samānayā (syā.).

They were declared by the Buddha's knowledge, being the same as the rule on a journey.

Addhānasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on the Origination of a Journey is concluded.

9. Theyyasatthasamuṭṭhānaṃ

9. 9. The Chapter on the Origination of Theft and a Weapon

266.

266.

Theyyasatthaṃ [V 0.0185] upassuti, sūpaviññāpanena ca;

Rattichannañca okāsaṃ, ete byūhena sattamā.

The training rule on travelling with thieves, the training rule on eavesdropping, the training rule on requesting curry and rice, the training rule on the darkness of night, the training rule on a concealed place, the training rule on an open space, and the seventh, the training rule on a lane.

Kāyacittena jāyanti, na te jāyanti vācato;

Tīhi dvārehi jāyanti, dvisamuṭṭhānikā ime.

These arise from body and mind; they do not arise from speech. They also arise from the three doors. These are of two origins.

Theyyasatthasamuṭṭhānā, desitādiccabandhunā.

The origins of the Theft and Weapon group were taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.

Theyyasatthasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on the Origination of Theft and a Weapon is concluded.

10. Dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhānaṃ

10. 10. The Chapter on the Origination of Teaching the Dhamma

267.

267.

Chattapāṇissa saddhammaṃ, na desenti tathāgatā;

Evameva tatheva (sī. syā.) daṇḍapāṇissa, satthaāvudhapāṇinaṃ.

The Tathāgatas do not teach the good Dhamma to one with an umbrella in hand; likewise to one with a staff in hand, or to those with a sword or weapon in hand.

Pādukupāhanā yānaṃ, seyyapallatthikāya ca;

Veṭhitoguṇṭhito ceva, ekādasamanūnakā.

Nor to one wearing sandals or shoes, in a vehicle, on a bed, or sitting with knees clasped; nor to one with head wrapped or covered. These training rules are eleven in full.

Vācācittena jāyanti, na te jāyanti kāyato;

Sabbe ekasamuṭṭhānā, samakā dhammadesane.

They arise from speech and mind; they do not arise from the body. All are of a single origin, the same as the rule on teaching the Dhamma.

Dhammadesanāsamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on the Origination of Teaching the Dhamma is concluded.

11. Bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānaṃ

11. 11. The Chapter on the Origination of Announcing a Fact

268.

268.

Bhūtaṃ [M 0.0163] kāyena jāyati, na vācā na ca cittato;

Vācato ca samuṭṭhāti, na kāyā na ca cittato.

The offense of announcing a fact arises from the body, not from speech, and not from mind; and it arises from speech, not from the body, and not from mind.

Kāyavācāya [V 0.0186] jāyati, na tu jāyati cittato;

Bhūtārocanakā [T 0.0231] nāma, tīhi ṭhānehi jāyati.

It arises from body and speech, but does not arise from mind. The so-called offense of announcing a fact arises from three bases.

Bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Chapter on the Origination of Announcing a Fact is concluded.

12. Corivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhānaṃ

12. 12. The Chapter on the Origination of Ordaining a Female Thief

269.

269.

Corī vācāya cittena, na taṃ jāyati kāyato;

Jāyati tīhi dvārehi, corivuṭṭhāpanaṃ idaṃ;

Akataṃ dvisamuṭṭhānaṃ, dhammarājena bhāsitaṃ ṭhapitaṃ (syā.).

The offense of ordaining a female thief arises from speech and mind; it does not arise from the body. It also arises from the three doors. This rule on ordaining a female thief was spoken by the King of Dhamma as being of two origins.

Corivuṭṭhāpanasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Arising from Ordaining a Female Thief is concluded.

13. Ananuññātasamuṭṭhānaṃ

13. 13. The Arising from [Acting] without Permission.

270.

270.

Ananuññātaṃ vācāya, na kāyā na ca cittato;

Jāyati kāyavācāya, na taṃ jāyati cittato.

The [offense of acting] without permission arises from speech, not from the body, and not from the mind; it arises from body and speech, but does not arise from the mind.

Jāyati vācācittena, na taṃ jāyati kāyato;

Jāyati [P 5.0090] tīhi dvārehi, akataṃ catuṭhānikaṃ.

It arises from speech and mind; it does not arise from the body. It arises from the three doors. It is of four origins.

Ananuññātasamuṭṭhānaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Section on the Arising from [Acting] without Permission is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānañhi saṅkhepaṃ, dasa tīṇi sudesitaṃ;

Asammohakaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, nettidhammānulomikaṃ;

Dhārayanto imaṃ viññū, samuṭṭhāne na muyhatīti.

Indeed, these thirteen origins have been well taught in brief; a basis for non-bewilderment, in accordance with the method of the Dhamma. The wise person who bears this in mind is not bewildered about the origins.

Samuṭṭhānasīsasaṅkhepo niṭṭhito.

The Summary Chapter on the Origins is concluded.

Antarapeyyālaṃ

The Intermediate Section

Katipucchāvāro

The Section of Questions on Number

271. Kati [T 0.0232][P 5.0091][M 0.0164][V 0.0187] āpattiyo? Kati āpattikkhandhā? Kati vinītavatthūni? Kati agāravā? Kati gāravā? Kati vinītavatthūni? Kati vipattiyo? Kati āpattisamuṭṭhānā? Kati vivādamūlāni? Kati anuvādamūlāni? Kati sāraṇīyā dhammā? Kati bhedakaravatthūni? Kati adhikaraṇāni? Kati samathā?

271. How many offenses? How many aggregates of offenses? How many settled matters? How many kinds of irreverence? How many kinds of reverence? How many settled matters? How many failures? How many origins of offenses? How many roots of disputes? How many roots of accusations? How many principles of cordiality? How many grounds for schism? How many legal issues? How many means of settlement?

Pañca āpattiyo. Pañca āpattikkhandhā. Pañca vinītavatthūni. Satta āpattiyo. Satta āpattikkhandhā. Satta vinītavatthūni. Cha agāravā. Cha gāravā. Cha vinītavatthūni. Catasso vipattiyo. Cha āpattisamuṭṭhānā. Cha vivādamūlāni. Cha anuvādamūlāni. Cha sāraṇīyā dhammā. Aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni. Cattāri adhikaraṇāni. Satta samathā.

There are five offenses. Five aggregates of offenses. Five settled matters. Seven offenses. Seven aggregates of offenses. Seven settled matters. Six kinds of irreverence. Six kinds of reverence. Six settled matters. Four failures. Six origins of offenses. Six roots of disputes. Six roots of accusations. Six principles of cordiality. Eighteen grounds for schism. Four legal issues. Seven means of settlement.

Tattha katamā pañca āpattiyo? Pārājikāpatti, saṅghādisesāpatti, pācittiyāpatti, pāṭidesanīyāpatti, dukkaṭāpatti – imā pañca āpattiyo.

Therein, what are the five offenses? The offense of defeat, the offense entailing a formal meeting, the offense entailing expiation, the offense entailing acknowledgment, the offense of wrong-doing—these are the five offenses.

Tattha katame pañca āpattikkhandhā? Pārājikāpattikkhandho, saṅghādisesāpattikkhandho, pācittiyāpattikkhandho, pāṭidesanīyāpattikkhandho, dukkaṭāpattikkhandho – ime pañca āpattikkhandhā.

Therein, what are the five aggregates of offenses? The aggregate of offenses of defeat, the aggregate of offenses entailing a formal meeting, the aggregate of offenses entailing expiation, the aggregate of offenses entailing acknowledgment, the aggregate of offenses of wrong-doing—these are the five aggregates of offenses.

Tattha [T 0.0233] katamāni pañca vinītavatthūni? Pañcahi āpattikkhandhehi ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī akiriyā akaraṇaṃ anajjhāpatti velāanatikkamo setughāto – imāni pañca vinītavatthūni.

Therein, what are the five settled matters? From the five aggregates of offenses: abstention, refraining, desisting, restraint, non-action, non-commission, not falling into an offense, not transgressing the boundary, the destruction of the bridge—these are the five settled matters.

Tattha [V 0.0188] katamā satta āpattiyo? Pārājikāpatti, saṅghādisesāpatti, thullaccayāpatti, pācittiyāpatti, pāṭidesanīyāpatti, dukkaṭāpatti, dubbhāsitāpatti – imā satta āpattiyo.

Therein, what are the seven offenses? The offense of defeat, the offense entailing a formal meeting, the grave offense, the offense entailing expiation, the offense entailing acknowledgment, the offense of wrong-doing, the offense of wrong speech—these are the seven offenses.

Tattha katame satta āpattikkhandhā? Pārājikāpattikkhandho, saṅghādisesāpattikkhandho, thullaccayāpattikkhandho, pācittiyāpattikkhandho, pāṭidesanīyāpattikkhandho, dukkaṭāpattikkhandho, dubbhāsitāpattikkhandho – ime satta āpattikkhandhā.

Therein, what are the seven aggregates of offenses? The aggregate of offenses of defeat, the aggregate of offenses entailing a formal meeting, the aggregate of grave offenses, the aggregate of offenses entailing expiation, the aggregate of offenses entailing acknowledgment, the aggregate of offenses of wrong-doing, the aggregate of offenses of wrong speech—these are the seven aggregates of offenses.

Tattha [M 0.0165] katamāni satta vinītavatthūni? Sattahi āpattikkhandhehi ārati virati paṭivirati veramaṇī akiriyā akaraṇaṃ anajjhāpatti velāanatikkamo setughāto – imāni satta vinītavatthūni.

Therein, what are the seven settled matters? From the seven aggregates of offenses: abstention, refraining, desisting, restraint, non-action, non-commission, not falling into an offense, not transgressing the boundary, the destruction of the bridge—these are the seven settled matters.

Tattha [P 5.0092] katame cha agāravā? Buddhe agāravo, dhamme agāravo, saṅghe agāravo, sikkhāya agāravo, appamāde agāravo, paṭisandhāre agāravo – ime cha agāravā.

Therein, what are the six kinds of irreverence? Irreverence toward the Buddha, irreverence toward the Dhamma, irreverence toward the Saṅgha, irreverence toward the training, irreverence toward heedfulness, irreverence toward friendly welcome—these are the six kinds of irreverence.

Tattha katame cha gāravā? Buddhe gāravo, dhamme gāravo, saṅghe gāravo, sikkhāya gāravo, appamāde gāravo, paṭisandhāre gāravo – ime cha gāravā.

Therein, what are the six kinds of reverence? Reverence toward the Buddha, reverence toward the Dhamma, reverence toward the Saṅgha, reverence toward the training, reverence toward heedfulness, reverence toward friendly welcome—these are the six kinds of reverence.

Tattha katamāni cha vinītavatthūni? Chahi agāravehi ārati virati paṭivirati [T 0.0234] veramaṇī akiriyā akaraṇaṃ anajjhāpatti velāanatikkamo setughāto – imāni cha vinītavatthūni.

Therein, what are the six settled matters? From the six kinds of irreverence: abstention, refraining, desisting, restraint, non-action, non-commission, not falling into an offense, not transgressing the boundary, the destruction of the bridge—these are the six settled matters.

Tattha katamā catasso vipattiyo? Sīlavipatti, ācāravipatti, diṭṭhivipatti, ājīvavipatti – imā catasso vipattiyo.

Therein, what are the four failures? Failure in moral virtue, failure in conduct, failure in view, failure in livelihood—these are the four failures.

Tattha katame cha āpattisamuṭṭhānā? Atthāpatti kāyato samuṭṭhāti, na vācato na cittato; atthāpatti vācato samuṭṭhāti, na kāyato na cittato; atthāpatti kāyato ca vācato ca samuṭṭhāti, na cittato; atthāpatti kāyato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhāti, na vācato; atthāpatti vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhāti, na kāyato; atthāpatti kāyato ca vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhāti – ime cha āpattisamuṭṭhānā.

Therein, what are the six origins of offenses? There is an offense that arises from the body, not from speech, not from the mind. There is an offense that arises from speech, not from the body, not from the mind. There is an offense that arises from the body and from speech, not from the mind. There is an offense that arises from the body and from the mind, not from speech. There is an offense that arises from speech and from the mind, not from the body. There is an offense that arises from the body, from speech, and from the mind. These are the six origins of offenses.

272. Tattha [V 0.0189] cūḷava. 216; a. ni. 6.36; ma. ni. 3.44; dī. ni. 3.325 katamāni cha vivādamūlāni? Idha bhikkhu kodhano hoti upanāhī. Yo so bhikkhu kodhano hoti upanāhī so sattharipi agāravo viharati appatisso, dhammepi agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghepi agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāyapi na paripūrakārī hoti. Yo so bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso, dhamme…pe… saṅghe…pe… sikkhāya na paripūrakārī, so saṅghe vivādaṃ janeti. Yo hoti vivādo bahujanāhitāya bahujanāsukhāya bahuno janassa anatthāya ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānaṃ. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā [T 0.0235] bahiddhā vā samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe [M 0.0166] tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa pahānāya vāyameyyātha. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā na samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavāya paṭipajjeyyātha. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa pahānaṃ hoti. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavo hoti.

272. Therein, what are the six roots of disputes? Here, a monk is angry and bears grudges. That monk who is angry and bears grudges dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, dwells without reverence and deference toward the Dhamma, dwells without reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha, and does not completely fulfill the training. That monk who dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, toward the Dhamma… toward the Saṅgha… and does not completely fulfill the training, he generates a dispute in the Saṅgha. That dispute is for the non-benefit of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the disadvantage, non-benefit, and suffering of gods and humans. If you should perceive such a root of dispute within yourself or externally, you should then strive for the abandoning of that same evil root of dispute. If you should not perceive such a root of dispute within yourself or externally, you should then practice for the non-occurrence in the future of that same evil root of dispute. Thus there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute. Thus there is the non-occurrence in the future of this evil root of dispute.

cūḷava. 216 Puna caparaṃ bhikkhu makkhī hoti paḷāsī…pe… issukī hoti maccharī, saṭho hoti māyāvī, pāpiccho hoti micchādiṭṭhi, sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī. Yo so bhikkhu sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī so sattharipi agāravo viharati appatisso, dhammepi agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghepi agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāyapi na paripūrakārī hoti. Yo so bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso dhamme…pe… saṅghe…pe… sikkhāya na paripūrakārī, so saṅghe vivādaṃ janeti. Yo so hoti vivādo bahujanāhitāya bahujanāsukhāya bahuno janassa anatthāya ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānaṃ. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa [T 0.0236] pahānāya vāyameyyātha. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā na samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavāya paṭipajjeyyātha. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa pahānaṃ hoti. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavo hoti. Imāni cha vivādamūlāni.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu is one who effaces the good deeds of others and is competitive... he is envious and stingy; he is deceitful and fraudulent; he has evil desires and wrong view; he is one who misapprehends his own views, holds on to them firmly, and relinquishes them with difficulty. A bhikkhu who misapprehends his own views, holds on to them firmly, and relinquishes them with difficulty, dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, without reverence and deference toward the Dhamma, without reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha, and is not one who fulfills the training. A bhikkhu who dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, toward the Dhamma, toward the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training, generates disputes in the Saṅgha. Such a dispute is for the non-welfare of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the harm of many people, and for the non-welfare and suffering of devas and humans. If you should see such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then you should strive for the abandoning of that evil root of dispute. If you should not see such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then you should practice for the non-occurrence of that evil root of dispute in the future. Thus there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute. Thus there is the non-occurrence of this evil root of dispute in the future. These are the six roots of dispute.

273. cūḷava. 217 Tattha katamāni cha anuvādamūlāni? Idha bhikkhu kodhano hoti upanāhī. Yo so bhikkhu kodhano hoti upanāhī so sattharipi agāravo viharati appatisso, dhammepi agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghepi agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāyapi na paripūrakārī hoti. Yo so bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso dhamme…pe… saṅghe [V 0.0190] …pe… sikkhāya na paripūrakārī so saṅghe anuvādaṃ janeti. Yo hoti anuvādo bahujanāhitāya bahujanāsukhāya bahuno janassa anatthāya ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānaṃ. Evarūpaṃ [M 0.0167] ce tumhe anuvādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe tasseva pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa pahānāya vāyameyyātha. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe anuvādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā na samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe tasseva pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavāya paṭipajjeyyātha. Evametassa pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa pahānaṃ hoti. Evametassa pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavo hoti.

273. Therein, what are the six roots of accusation? Here, a bhikkhu is wrathful and bears enmity. That bhikkhu who is wrathful and bears enmity dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, dwells without reverence and deference toward the Dhamma, dwells without reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha, and is not one who fulfills the training. That bhikkhu who dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training, generates accusation in the Saṅgha. Such an accusation is for the non-welfare of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the harm of many people, and for the non-welfare and suffering of devas and humans. If you should see such a root of accusation either internally or externally, then you should strive for the abandoning of that evil root of accusation. If you should not see such a root of accusation either internally or externally, then you should practice for the non-occurrence of that evil root of accusation in the future. Thus there is the abandoning of this evil root of accusation. Thus there is the non-occurrence of this evil root of accusation in the future.

Puna caparaṃ bhikkhu makkhī hoti palāsī…pe… issukī hoti maccharī, saṭho hoti māyāvī, pāpiccho hoti micchādiṭṭhi, sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī [T 0.0237] hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī. Yo so bhikkhu sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī so sattharipi agāravo viharati appatisso, dhammepi agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghepi agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāyapi na paripūrakārī hoti. Yo bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso dhamme…pe… saṅghe…pe… sikkhāya na paripūrakārī so saṅghe anuvādaṃ janeti. Yo hoti anuvādo bahujanāhitāya bahujanāsukhāya bahuno janassa anatthāya ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānaṃ. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe anuvādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe tasseva pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa pahānāya vāyameyyātha. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe anuvādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā na samanupasseyyātha tatra tumhe tasseva pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavāya paṭipajjeyyātha. Evametassa pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa pahānaṃ hoti. Evametassa pāpakassa anuvādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavo hoti. Imāni cha anuvādamūlāni.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu is one who effaces the good deeds of others and is competitive... he is envious and stingy; he is deceitful and fraudulent; he has evil desires and wrong view; he is one who misapprehends his own views, holds on to them firmly, and relinquishes them with difficulty. A bhikkhu who misapprehends his own views, holds on to them firmly, and relinquishes them with difficulty, dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, without reverence and deference toward the Dhamma, without reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha, and is not one who fulfills the training. A bhikkhu who dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, toward the Dhamma, toward the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training, generates accusation in the Saṅgha. Such an accusation is for the non-welfare of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the harm of many people, and for the non-welfare and suffering of devas and humans. If you should see such a root of accusation either internally or externally, then you should strive for the abandoning of that evil root of accusation. If you should not see such a root of accusation either internally or externally, then you should practice for the non-occurrence of that evil root of accusation in the future. Thus there is the abandoning of this evil root of accusation. Thus there is the non-occurrence of this evil root of accusation in the future. These are the six roots of accusation.

274. dī. ni. 3.324; a. ni. 6.11 Tattha katame cha sāraṇīyā dhammā? Idha bhikkhuno mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

274. Therein, what are the six states to be remembered? Here, a bhikkhu’s bodily action of loving-kindness toward his companions in the holy life is maintained both openly and in secret. This principle is memorable, endearing, and inspires respect; it conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

Puna caparaṃ bhikkhuno mettaṃ [T 0.0238] vacīkammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu’s verbal action of loving-kindness toward his companions in the holy life is maintained both openly and in secret. This principle is memorable, endearing, and inspires respect; it conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

Puna [M 0.0168][V 0.0191] caparaṃ bhikkhuno mettaṃ manokammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu’s mental action of loving-kindness toward his companions in the holy life is maintained both openly and in secret. This principle is memorable, endearing, and inspires respect; it conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

Puna caparaṃ bhikkhu ye te lābhā dhammikā dhammaladdhā antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampi tathārūpehi lābhehi appaṭivibhattabhogī hoti sīlavantehi sabrahmacārīhi sādhāraṇabhogī. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu is one who enjoys without reservation such gains as are righteous and righteously obtained—even just the contents of his bowl—and enjoys them in common with his virtuous companions in the holy life. This principle is memorable, endearing, and inspires respect; it conduces to cohesion, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity.

Puna caparaṃ bhikkhu yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññupasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni[P 5.0093], tathārūpesu sīlesu sīlasāmaññagato viharati sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, a monk dwells, in regard to those virtues that are unbroken, unperforated, unspotted, unblotched, liberating, praised by the wise, unmisapprehended, and conducive to concentration, as one who has attained to sameness in virtue with his fellows in the holy life, both openly and in private. This principle, too, is to be remembered, making for endearment and respect, and conducing to cohesion, non-dispute, concord, and unity.

Puna caparaṃ bhikkhu yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharati sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati. Ime cha sāraṇīyā dhammā.

Furthermore, a monk dwells, in regard to that view which is noble, emancipating, and which leads out one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering, as one who has attained to sameness in view with his fellows in the holy life, both openly and in private. This principle, too, is to be remembered, making for endearment and respect, and conducing to cohesion, non-dispute, concord, and unity. These are the six memorable principles.

275. Tattha [T 0.0239] katamāni aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni? Idha bhikkhu adhammaṃ “dhammo”ti dīpeti, dhammaṃ “adhammo”ti dīpeti, avinayaṃ “vinayo”ti dīpeti, vinayaṃ “avinayo”ti dīpeti, abhāsitaṃ alapitaṃ tathāgatena “bhāsitaṃ lapitaṃ tathāgatenā”ti dīpeti, bhāsitaṃ lapitaṃ tathāgatena “abhāsitaṃ alapitaṃ tathāgatenā”ti dīpeti, anāciṇṇaṃ tathāgatena “āciṇṇaṃ tathāgatenā”ti dīpeti, āciṇṇaṃ tathāgatena “anāciṇṇaṃ tathāgatenā”ti dīpeti, apaññattaṃ tathāgatena “paññattaṃ tathāgatenā”ti dīpeti, paññattaṃ tathāgatena “apaññattaṃ tathāgatenā”ti dīpeti, āpattiṃ “anāpattī”ti dīpeti, anāpattiṃ “āpattī”ti dīpeti, lahukaṃ āpattiṃ “garukā āpattī”ti dīpeti, garukaṃ āpattiṃ “lahukā āpattī”ti dīpeti, sāvasesaṃ āpattiṃ “anavasesā āpattī”ti [V 0.0192] dīpeti, anavasesaṃ āpattiṃ “sāvasesā āpattī”ti [M 0.0169] dīpeti, duṭṭhullaṃ āpattiṃ “aduṭṭhullā āpattī”ti dīpeti, aduṭṭhullaṃ āpattiṃ “duṭṭhullā āpattī”ti dīpeti. Imāni aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni.

275. Therein, what are the eighteen grounds for creating a schism? Here, a monk declares what is not the Dhamma as the Dhamma, and the Dhamma as not the Dhamma; he declares what is not the Vinaya as the Vinaya, and the Vinaya as not the Vinaya; he declares what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata, and what was spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata; he declares what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata, and what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata; he declares what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as prescribed by the Tathāgata, and what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as not prescribed by the Tathāgata; he declares an offense as a non-offense, and a non-offense as an offense; he declares a light offense as a grave offense, and a grave offense as a light offense; he declares an offense with a remainder as an offense without a remainder, and an offense without a remainder as an offense with a remainder; he declares a gross offense as a non-gross offense, and a non-gross offense as a gross offense. These are the eighteen grounds for creating a schism.

cūḷava. 215; pari. 340 Tattha katamāni cattāri adhikaraṇāni? Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ, anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ, kiccādhikaraṇaṃ – imāni cattāri adhikaraṇāni.

Therein, what are the four legal questions? The legal question of dispute, the legal question of accusation, the legal question of an offense, and the legal question of duties. These are the four legal questions.

Tattha katame satta samathā? Sammukhāvinayo, sativinayo, amūḷhavinayo, paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ, yebhuyyasikā, tassapāpiyasikā, tiṇavatthārako [T 0.0240] – ime satta samathā.

Therein, what are the seven settlements? Settlement in the presence, settlement by mindfulness, settlement for one who has recovered sanity, acting according to what is acknowledged, decision by majority, a verdict of specific depravity, and covering over as with grass. These are the seven settlements.

Katipucchāvāro niṭṭhito.

The Section of Questions is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Āpatti āpattikkhandhā, vinītā sattadhā puna;

Vinītāgāravā ceva, gāravā mūlameva ca.

Offense, groups of offenses, settled matters, and again the sevenfold; settled matters, disrespect and respect, and the very root.

Puna vinītā vipatti, samuṭṭhānā vivādanā;

Anuvādā sāraṇīyaṃ, bhedādhikaraṇena ca.

Again settled matters, failure, origins of offenses, disputes, accusations, memorable principles, grounds for schism, and legal questions.

Satteva samathā vuttā, padā sattarasā imeti.

The seven settlements have been taught; these topics are seventeen in all.

1. Chaāpattisamuṭṭhānavāro

1. The Section on the Six Origins of an Offense

276. Paṭhamena [T 0.0241] āpattisamuṭṭhānena pārājikaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Na hīti vattabbaṃ. Saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Thullaccayaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Pācittiyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Pāṭidesanīyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Dukkaṭaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Dubbhāsitaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Na hīti vattabbaṃ.

276. By the first origin of an offense, would one incur a pārājika offense? It should be said: Certainly not. Would one incur a saṅghādisesa offense? It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a thullaccaya offense? It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a pācittiya offense? It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a pāṭidesanīya offense? It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a dukkaṭa offense? It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a dubbhāsita offense? It should be said: Certainly not.

Dutiyena āpattisamuṭṭhānena pārājikaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Na hīti vattabbaṃ. Saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Thullaccayaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Pācittiyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Pāṭidesanīyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Na hīti vattabbaṃ. Dukkaṭaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Dubbhāsitaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Na hīti vattabbaṃ.

It should be said: Certainly not. Would one incur a dukkaṭa offense? It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a dubbhāsita offense? It should be said: Certainly not.

Pācittiyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Pāṭidesanīyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Dukkaṭaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Dubbhāsitaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Na hīti vattabbaṃ.

It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a dukkaṭa offense? It should be said: It is possible. Would one incur a dubbhāsita offense? It should be said: Certainly not.

Chaṭṭhena āpattisamuṭṭhānena pārājikaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Saṅghādisesaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Thullaccayaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Pācittiyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Pāṭidesanīyaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Dukkaṭaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Siyāti vattabbaṃ. Dubbhāsitaṃ āpajjeyyāti? Na hīti vattabbaṃ.

Through the sixth origin of an offense, would one incur a pārājika offense? It should be said: One would. Would one incur a saṅghādisesa offense? It should be said: One would. Would one incur a thullaccaya offense? It should be said: One would. Would one incur a pācittiya offense? It should be said: One would. Would one incur a pāṭidesanīya offense? It should be said: One would. Would one incur a dukkaṭa offense? It should be said: One would. Would one incur a dubbhāsita offense? It should be said: One would not.

Chaāpattisamuṭṭhānavāro niṭṭhito paṭhamo.

The First Section on the Six Origins of an Offense is concluded.

2. Katāpattivāro

2. The Section on Committed Offenses

277. Paṭhamena āpattisamuṭṭhānena kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Paṭhamena [T 0.0243] āpattisamuṭṭhānena pañca āpattiyo āpajjati. Bhikkhu kappiyasaññī saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karoti adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ, payoge dukkaṭaṃ; ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgate āpatti [M 0.0171] thullaccayassa; tasmiṃ piṇḍe āgate āpatti saṅghādisesassa; bhikkhu kappiyasaññī vikāle bhojanaṃ bhuñjati, āpatti pācittiyassa; bhikkhu kappiyasaññī aññātikāya [V 0.0194] bhikkhuniyā antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhāya hatthato khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā sahatthā paṭiggahetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pāṭidesanīyassa – paṭhamena āpattisamuṭṭhānena imā pañca āpattiyo āpajjati.

277. How many offenses are incurred through the first origin of an offense? Through the first origin of an offense, five offenses are incurred. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, builds a hut by his own solicitation, without having the site designated, exceeding the prescribed size, on a site with living beings, and without a surrounding space—there is an offense of wrong conduct in the effort. Before one clod of earth arrives, there is a grave offense; when that clod of earth arrives, there is a saṅghādisesa offense. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, eats food at the wrong time—there is a pācittiya offense. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, receives and eats with his own hand hard or soft food from the hand of a nun who is not a relative and who has entered an inhabited area—there is a pāṭidesanīya offense. Through the first origin of an offense, these five offenses are incurred.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti? Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ katihi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā? Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ katihi samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhanti? Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ katamaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ? Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ dve vipattiyo bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ, siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ pañcahi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā saṅghādisesāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā pāṭidesanīyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – kāyato samuṭṭhanti, na vācato na cittato. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ[T 0.0244]. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

To how many of the four kinds of failures do these offenses belong? By how many of the seven aggregates of offenses are they included? From how many of the six origins of offenses do they arise? Which of the four kinds of legal issues is it? By how many of the seven methods of settlement are they settled? These offenses belong to two of the four kinds of failures—it may be a failure in virtue, or it may be a failure in conduct. They are included in five of the seven aggregates of offenses—it may be by the saṅghādisesa aggregate of offenses, by the grave offense aggregate, by the pācittiya aggregate of offenses, by the pāṭidesanīya aggregate of offenses, or by the aggregate of offenses of wrong conduct. They arise from one of the six origins of offenses—they arise from the body, not from speech, not from mind. Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. They are settled by three of the seven methods of settlement—it may be by settlement in the presence and by acknowledgment, or by settlement in the presence and by covering over with grass.

278. Dutiyena āpattisamuṭṭhānena kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Dutiyena āpattisamuṭṭhānena catasso āpattiyo āpajjati – bhikkhu kappiyasaññī samādisati [P 5.0095] – “kuṭiṃ me karothā”ti. Tassa kuṭiṃ karonti adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ. Payoge dukkaṭaṃ; ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgate āpatti thullaccayassa; tasmiṃ piṇḍe āgate āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Bhikkhu kappiyasaññī anupasampannaṃ padaso dhammaṃ vāceti, āpatti pācittiyassa – dutiyena āpattisamuṭṭhānena imā catasso āpattiyo āpajjati.

278. How many offenses are incurred through the second origin of an offense? Through the second origin of an offense, four offenses are incurred. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, directs: "Build a hut for me." They build him a hut without having the site designated, exceeding the prescribed size, on a site with living beings, and without a surrounding space. There is an offense of wrong conduct in the effort; before one clod of earth arrives, there is a grave offense; when that clod of earth arrives, there is a saṅghādisesa offense. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, teaches the Dhamma word by word to one who is unordained—there is a pācittiya offense. Through the second origin of an offense, these four offenses are incurred.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ dve vipattiyo bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ, siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ [M 0.0172] catūhi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā saṅghādisesāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – vācato samuṭṭhanti, na kāyato na cittato. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena [T 0.0245] ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

To how many of the four kinds of failures do those offenses belong… and so on… by how many of the seven methods of settlement are they settled? Those offenses belong to two of the four kinds of failures—it may be a failure in virtue, or it may be a failure in conduct. They are included in four of the seven aggregates of offenses—it may be by the saṅghādisesa aggregate of offenses, by the grave offense aggregate, by the pācittiya aggregate of offenses, or by the aggregate of offenses of wrong conduct. They arise from one of the six origins of offenses—they arise from speech, not from body, not from mind. Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. They are settled by three of the seven methods of settlement—it may be by settlement in the presence and by acknowledgment, or by settlement in the presence and by covering over with grass.

279. Tatiyena [V 0.0195] āpattisamuṭṭhānena kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Tatiyena āpattisamuṭṭhānena pañca āpattiyo āpajjati. Bhikkhu kappiyasaññī saṃvidahitvā kuṭiṃ karoti adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ. Payoge dukkaṭaṃ; ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgate āpatti thullaccayassa; tasmiṃ piṇḍe āgate āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Bhikkhu kappiyasaññī paṇītabhojanāni attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pācittiyassa. Bhikkhu kappiyasaññī bhikkhuniyā vosāsantiyā na nivāretvā bhuñjati, āpatti pāṭidesanīyassa – tatiyena āpattisamuṭṭhānena imā pañca āpattiyo āpajjati.

279. How many offenses are incurred through the third origin of an offense? Through the third origin of an offense, five offenses are incurred. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, having made arrangements, builds a hut without having the site designated, exceeding the prescribed size, on a site with living beings, and without a surrounding space. There is an offense of wrong conduct in the effort; before one clod of earth arrives, there is a grave offense; when that clod of earth arrives, there is a saṅghādisesa offense. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, eats choice foods after requesting them for his own benefit—there is a pācittiya offense. A monk, perceiving it as allowable, eats without preventing a nun who is giving instructions—there is a pāṭidesanīya offense. Through the third origin of an offense, these five offenses are incurred.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ dve vipattiyo bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ, siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ pañcahi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā saṅghādisesāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā pāṭidesanīyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – kāyato ca vācato ca samuṭṭhanti, na cittato. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ[T 0.0246]. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

To how many of the four kinds of failures do those offenses belong…pe… by how many of the seven methods of settlement are they settled? Those offenses belong to two of the four kinds of failures—it may be a failure in virtue, or it may be a failure in conduct. They are included in five of the seven aggregates of offenses—it may be by the aggregate of saṅghādisesa offenses, by the aggregate of grave offenses, by the aggregate of pācittiya offenses, by the aggregate of pāṭidesanīya offenses, or by the aggregate of offenses of wrong conduct. They arise from one of the six origins of offenses—they arise from body and speech, but not from mind. Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. They are settled by three of the seven methods of settlement—it may be by settlement in the presence and by acknowledgment, or by settlement in the presence and by covering over with grass.

280. Catutthena āpattisamuṭṭhānena kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Catutthena āpattisamuṭṭhānena cha āpattiyo āpajjati – bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati, āpatti pārājikassa; bhikkhu akappiyasaññī saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karoti [P 5.0096] adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ, payoge [M 0.0173] dukkaṭaṃ; ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgate āpatti thullaccayassa; tasmiṃ piṇḍe āgate āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Bhikkhu akappiyasaññī vikāle bhojanaṃ bhuñjati, āpatti pācittiyassa. Bhikkhu akappiyasaññī aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhāya hatthato khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā sahatthā paṭiggahetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pāṭidesanīyassa. Catutthena āpattisamuṭṭhānena imā cha āpattiyo āpajjati.

280. How many offenses are incurred through the fourth origin of offenses? Through the fourth origin of offenses, six offenses are incurred. A monk engages in sexual intercourse: there is an offense of pārājika. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, builds a hut requested by himself, with an undesignated site, exceeding the measure, with dangers, and without a surrounding space: there is an offense of wrong conduct in the effort; before one clod of earth arrives, there is an offense of a grave offense; when that clod of earth has arrived, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, eats food at the wrong time: there is an offense of pācittiya. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, receives with his own hand and eats hard or soft food from the hand of a nun who is not a relative and who has entered an inhabited area: there is an offense of pāṭidesanīya. Through the fourth origin of offenses, these six offenses are incurred.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ dve vipattiyo bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ[V 0.0196], siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ chahi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā pārājikāpattikkhandhena, siyā saṅghādisesāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā pāṭidesanīyāpattikkhandhena[T 0.0247], siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – kāyato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti, na vācato. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

To how many of the four kinds of failures do those offenses belong? …pe… By how many of the seven methods of settlement are they settled? Those offenses belong to two of the four kinds of failures: it may be a failure in virtue, or it may be a failure in conduct. They are included in six of the seven aggregates of offenses: it may be by the aggregate of pārājika offenses, by the aggregate of saṅghādisesa offenses, by the aggregate of grave offenses, by the aggregate of pācittiya offenses, by the aggregate of pāṭidesanīya offenses, or by the aggregate of offenses of wrong conduct. Of the six origins of offenses, they arise from one origin: they arise from body and from mind, not from speech. Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. Of the seven methods of settlement, they are settled by three methods of settlement: it may be by settlement in the presence and by acknowledgment, or it may be by settlement in the presence and by covering over with grass.

281. Pañcamena āpattisamuṭṭhānena kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Pañcamena āpattisamuṭṭhānena cha āpattiyo āpajjati. Bhikkhu pāpiccho icchāpakato asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapati, āpatti pārājikassa; bhikkhu akappiyasaññī samādisati – “kuṭiṃ me karothā”ti. Tassa kuṭiṃ karonti adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ. Payoge dukkaṭaṃ; ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgate āpatti thullaccayassa; tasmiṃ piṇḍe āgate āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Bhikkhu akappiyasaññī anupasampannaṃ padaso dhammaṃ vāceti, āpatti pācittiyassa. Na khuṃsetukāmo na vambhetukāmo na maṅkukattukāmo davakamyatā hīnena hīnaṃ vadeti, āpatti dubbhāsitassa – pañcamena āpattisamuṭṭhānena imā cha āpattiyo āpajjati.

281. How many offenses are incurred through the fifth origin of offenses? Through the fifth origin of offenses, six offenses are incurred. A monk, having evil wishes and being overcome by them, boasts of a non-existent, untrue superhuman state: there is an offense of pārājika. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, instructs: ‘Build a hut for me.’ They build a hut for him with an undesignated site, exceeding the measure, with dangers, and without a surrounding space. In the effort, there is an offense of wrong conduct; before one clod of earth arrives, there is an offense of a grave offense; when that clod of earth has arrived, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, makes one who is not fully ordained recite the Dhamma word by word: there is an offense of pācittiya. Not wishing to abuse, not wishing to disparage, not wishing to humiliate, but out of a desire for sport, one speaks of a base thing with base speech: there is an offense of wrong speech. Through the fifth origin of offenses, these six offenses are incurred.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ [M 0.0174] dve vipattiyo bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ, siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ chahi āpattikkhandhehi [T 0.0248] saṅgahitā – siyā pārājikāpattikkhandhena, siyā saṅghādisesāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena, siyā dubbhāsitāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti, na kāyato. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

To how many of the four kinds of failures do those offenses belong? …pe… By how many of the seven methods of settlement are they settled? Those offenses belong to two of the four kinds of failures: it may be a failure in virtue, or it may be a failure in conduct. They are included in six of the seven aggregates of offenses: it may be by the aggregate of pārājika offenses, by the aggregate of saṅghādisesa offenses, by the aggregate of grave offenses, by the aggregate of pācittiya offenses, by the aggregate of offenses of wrong conduct, or by the aggregate of offenses of wrong speech. Of the six origins of offenses, they arise from one origin: they arise from speech and from mind, not from body. Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. Of the seven methods of settlement, they are settled by three methods of settlement: it may be by settlement in the presence and by acknowledgment, or it may be by settlement in the presence and by covering over with grass.

282. Chaṭṭhena āpattisamuṭṭhānena kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Chaṭṭhena āpattisamuṭṭhānena cha āpattiyo āpajjati – bhikkhu saṃvidahitvā bhaṇḍaṃ avaharati, āpatti [V 0.0197] pārājikassa[P 5.0097]; bhikkhu akappiyasaññī saṃvidahitvā kuṭiṃ karoti adesitavatthukaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ sārambhaṃ aparikkamanaṃ, payoge dukkaṭaṃ; ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ anāgate āpatti thullaccayassa; tasmiṃ piṇḍe āgate, āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Bhikkhu akappiyasaññī paṇītabhojanāni attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pācittiyassa. Bhikkhu akappiyasaññī bhikkhuniyā vosāsantiyā na nivāretvā bhuñjati, āpatti pāṭidesanīyassa – chaṭṭhena āpattisamuṭṭhānena imā cha āpattiyo āpajjati.

282. How many offenses are incurred through the sixth origin of offenses? Through the sixth origin of offenses, six offenses are incurred. A monk, having conspired, steals goods: it is an offense of pārājika. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, having conspired, builds a hut with an undesignated site, exceeding the measure, with dangers, and without a surrounding space: in the effort, it is an offense of dukkaṭa; before one clod of earth arrives, it is an offense of thullaccaya; when that clod of earth has arrived, it is an offense of saṅghādisesa. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, having requested fine foods for his own sake, eats them: it is an offense of pācittiya. A monk, perceiving it as unallowable, eats without stopping a nun who is directing: it is an offense of pāṭidesanīya. Through the sixth origin of offenses, these six offenses are incurred.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti? Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ katihi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā[T 0.0249]? Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ katihi āpattisamuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhanti? Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ katamaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ? Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ dve vipattiyo bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ, siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ chahi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā pārājikāpattikkhandhena, siyā saṅghādisesāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā pāṭidesanīyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – kāyato ca vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ [M 0.0175] samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena cāti.

Of the four failures, to how many failures do those offenses belong? Of the seven groups of offenses, by how many groups of offenses are they included? Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins do they arise? Of the four legal issues, which legal issue is it? Of the seven settlements, by how many settlements are they settled? Those offenses belong to two of the four failures: sometimes a failure in virtue, sometimes a failure in conduct. They are included in six of the seven groups of offenses: sometimes in the group of pārājika offenses, sometimes in the group of saṅghādisesa offenses, sometimes in the group of thullaccaya offenses, sometimes in the group of pācittiya offenses, sometimes in the group of pāṭidesanīya offenses, sometimes in the group of dukkaṭa offenses. Of the six origins of offenses, they arise from one origin: they arise from body, from speech, and from mind. Of the four legal issues, it is an offense-legal issue. Of the seven settlements, they are settled by three settlements: sometimes by settlement in the presence and by acting on an admission, and sometimes by settlement in the presence and by covering over with grass.

Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ

Of the six origins of offenses.

Katāpattivāro niṭṭhito dutiyo.

The Second Section on Incurred Offenses is finished.

3. Āpattisamuṭṭhānagāthā

3. 3. Verses on the Origins of Offenses

283.

283.

Samuṭṭhānā kāyikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā kati;

Pucchāmi taṃ brūhi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is bodily was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, how many offenses have arisen? O expert in the Vibhaṅgas, I ask you this. Tell me.

Samuṭṭhānā [V 0.0198] kāyikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā pañca;

Etaṃ [T 0.0250] te akkhāmi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is bodily was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, five offenses have arisen. This I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅgas.

Samuṭṭhānā vācasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā kati;

Pucchāmi taṃ brūhi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is verbal was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, how many offenses have arisen? O expert in the Vibhaṅgas, I ask you this. Tell me.

Samuṭṭhānā vācasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā catasso;

Etaṃ te akkhāmi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is verbal was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, four offenses have arisen. This I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅgas.

Samuṭṭhānā kāyikā vācasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā kati;

Pucchāmi [T 0.0251] taṃ brūhi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is from body and speech was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, how many offenses have arisen? O expert in the Vibhaṅgas, I ask you this. Tell me.

Samuṭṭhānā [M 0.0176] kāyikā vācasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā pañca;

Etaṃ te akkhāmi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is from body and speech was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, five offenses have arisen. This I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅgas.

Samuṭṭhānā kāyikā mānasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā kati;

Pucchāmi taṃ brūhi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is from body and mind was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, how many offenses have arisen? O expert in the Vibhaṅgas, I ask you this. Tell me.

Samuṭṭhānā [V 0.0199] kāyikā mānasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā cha;

Etaṃ te akkhāmi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is from body and mind was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, six offenses have arisen. This I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅgas.

Samuṭṭhānā vācasikā mānasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā kati;

Pucchāmi taṃ brūhi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is from speech and mind was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, how many offenses have arisen? O expert in the Vibhaṅgas, I ask you this. Tell me.

Samuṭṭhānā vācasikā mānasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā cha;

Etaṃ te akkhāmi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is from speech and mind was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, six offenses have arisen. This I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅgas.

Samuṭṭhānā kāyikā vācasikā mānasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā kati;

Pucchāmi taṃ brūhi vibhaṅgakovida.

That origin which is from body, speech, and mind was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, how many offenses have arisen? O expert in the Vibhaṅgas, I ask you this. Tell me.

Samuṭṭhānā [P 5.0098] kāyikā vācasikā mānasikā anantadassinā;

Akkhātā lokahitena vivekadassinā;

Āpattiyo tena samuṭṭhitā cha;

Etaṃ [T 0.0252] te akkhāmi vibhaṅgakovidāti.

That origin which is from body, speech, and mind was declared by the boundless seer, the seer of seclusion, the one who acts for the welfare of the world. From that origin, six offenses have arisen. This I declare to you, O expert in the Vibhaṅgas.

Āpattisamuṭṭhānagāthā niṭṭhitā tatiyā.

The third, the Verses on the Origins of Offenses, is finished.

4. Vipattipaccayavāro

4. 4. The Section on Failure as a Condition

284. Sīlavipattipaccayā [M 0.0177] kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Sīlavipattipaccayā catasso [V 0.0200] āpattiyo āpajjati – bhikkhunī jānaṃ pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicchādeti, āpatti pārājikassa; vematikā paṭicchādeti, āpatti thullaccayassa; bhikkhu saṅghādisesaṃ paṭicchādeti, āpatti pācittiyassa; attano duṭṭhullaṃ āpattiṃ paṭicchādeti, āpatti dukkaṭassa – sīlavipattipaccayā imā catasso āpattiyo āpajjati.

284. Due to the condition of corruption in virtue, how many offenses does one incur? Due to the condition of corruption in virtue, one incurs four offenses: if a bhikkhunī knowingly conceals a pārājika offense, it is an offense of pārājika; if, being in doubt, she conceals it, it is an offense of thullaccaya; if a bhikkhu conceals a saṅghādisesa offense, it is an offense of pācittiya; if one conceals one's own grave offense, it is an offense of dukkaṭa. Due to the condition of corruption in virtue, one incurs these four offenses.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ dve vipattiyo bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ, siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ catūhi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā pārājikāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – kāyato ca vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

Among the four corruptions, to how many corruptions do those offenses belong? … Among the seven principles of settlement, by how many principles of settlement are they settled? Among the four corruptions, those offenses belong to two corruptions: sometimes to corruption of virtue, sometimes to corruption of conduct. Among the seven classes of offenses, they are included in four classes of offenses: sometimes in the class of pārājika offenses, sometimes in the class of thullaccaya offenses, sometimes in the class of pācittiya offenses, sometimes in the class of dukkaṭa offenses. Among the six origins of offenses, they arise from one origin: they arise from body, speech, and mind. Among the four legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. Among the seven principles of settlement, they are settled by three principles of settlement: sometimes by settlement in the presence and by acting according to acknowledgment; sometimes by settlement in the presence and by covering with grass.

285. Ācāravipattipaccayā kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Ācāravipattipaccayā [T 0.0253] ekaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Ācāravipattiṃ paṭicchādeti, āpatti dukkaṭassa – ācāravipattipaccayā imaṃ ekaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati.

285. Due to the condition of corruption in conduct, how many offenses does one incur? Due to the condition of corruption in conduct, one incurs one offense. If one conceals a corruption of conduct, an offense of wrong conduct is incurred. Due to the condition of corruption in conduct, one incurs this one offense.

Sā āpatti catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajati …pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammati? Sā āpatti catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ ekaṃ vipattiṃ bhajati – ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ ekena āpattikkhandhena saṅgahitā – dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhāti – kāyato ca vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhāti. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammati – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

Among the four corruptions, to how many corruptions does that offense belong? … Among the seven principles of settlement, by how many principles of settlement is it settled? Among the four corruptions, that offense belongs to one corruption: the corruption of conduct. Among the seven classes of offenses, it is included in one class of offenses: the class of dukkaṭa offenses. Among the six origins of offenses, it arises from one origin: it arises from body, speech, and mind. Among the four legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. Among the seven principles of settlement, it is settled by three principles of settlement: sometimes by settlement in the presence and by acting according to acknowledgment; sometimes by settlement in the presence and by covering with grass.

286. Diṭṭhivipattipaccayā [M 0.0178] kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Diṭṭhivipattipaccayā dve āpattiyo āpajjati. Pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā yāvatatiyaṃ samanubhāsanāya na paṭinissajjati, ñattiyā dukkaṭaṃ ñattiyā dukkaṭaṃ, dvīhi kammavācāhi dukkaṭā (syā. ka.); kammavācāpariyosāne āpatti pācittiyassa – diṭṭhivipattipaccayā imā dve āpattiyo āpajjati.

286. Due to the condition of corruption in view, how many offenses does one incur? Due to the condition of corruption in view, one incurs two offenses. If, upon being admonished up to the third time for an evil view, one does not abandon it, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred at the motion; at the conclusion of the formal act, a pācittiya offense is incurred. Due to the condition of corruption in view, one incurs these two offenses.

Tā [V 0.0201] āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ ekaṃ vipattiṃ bhajanti – ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ dvīhi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā [P 5.0099] – siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena[T 0.0254], siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhanti – kāyato ca vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

Among the four corruptions, to how many corruptions do those offenses belong? … Among the seven principles of settlement, by how many principles of settlement are they settled? Among the four corruptions, those offenses belong to one corruption: the corruption of conduct. Among the seven classes of offenses, they are included in two classes of offenses: sometimes in the class of pācittiya offenses, sometimes in the class of dukkaṭa offenses. Among the six origins of offenses, they arise from one origin: they arise from body, speech, and mind. Among the four legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. Among the seven principles of settlement, they are settled by three principles of settlement: sometimes by settlement in the presence and by acting according to acknowledgment; sometimes by settlement in the presence and by covering with grass.

287. Ājīvavipattipaccayā kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Ājīvavipattipaccayā cha āpattiyo āpajjati – ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā pāpiccho icchāpakato asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapati, āpatti pārājikassa; ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā sañcarittaṃ samāpajjati, āpatti saṅghādisesassa; ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā “yo te vihāre vasati, so bhikkhu arahā”ti bhaṇati, paṭivijānantassa āpatti thullaccayassa; ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā bhikkhu paṇītabhojanāni attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pācittiyassa; ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā bhikkhunī paṇītabhojanāni attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pāṭidesanīyassa; ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā sūpaṃ vā odanaṃ vā agilāno attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti dukkaṭassa – ājīvavipattipaccayā imā cha āpattiyo āpajjati.

287. Due to the condition of corruption in livelihood, how many offenses does one incur? Due to the condition of corruption in livelihood, one incurs six offenses: for the sake of livelihood, on account of livelihood, being of evil wishes and overcome by desire, one speaks of a superhuman state that is non-existent and untrue, a pārājika offense is incurred; for the sake of livelihood, on account of livelihood, one engages in being a go-between, a saṅghādisesa offense is incurred; for the sake of livelihood, on account of livelihood, one says, ‘The bhikkhu who lives in your dwelling is an arahant,’ and when the listener understands, a thullaccaya offense is incurred; for the sake of livelihood, on account of livelihood, a bhikkhu, having requested choice foods for his own sake, consumes them, a pācittiya offense is incurred; for the sake of livelihood, on account of livelihood, a bhikkhunī, having requested choice foods for her own sake, consumes them, a pāṭidesanīya offense is incurred; for the sake of livelihood, on account of livelihood, one who is not ill, having requested soup or rice for one’s own sake, consumes it, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. Due to the condition of corruption in livelihood, one incurs these six offenses.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti. Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ dve [M 0.0179] vipattiyo [T 0.0255] bhajanti – siyā sīlavipattiṃ, siyā ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ chahi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā pārājikāpattikkhandhena, siyā saṅghādisesāpattikkhandhena, siyā thullaccayāpattikkhandhena, siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā pāṭidesanīyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ chahi samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhanti – siyā kāyato samuṭṭhanti, na vācato na cittato; siyā vācato samuṭṭhanti, na kāyato na cittato; siyā kāyato ca vācato ca samuṭṭhanti, na cittato; siyā kāyato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti, na vācato; siyā vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti, na kāyato; siyā kāyato ca vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi [V 0.0202] samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

Among the four corruptions, to how many corruptions do those offenses belong? … Among the seven principles of settlement, by how many principles of settlement are they settled? Those offenses belong to two of the four corruptions: sometimes to corruption of virtue, sometimes to corruption of conduct. They are included in six of the seven classes of offenses: sometimes in the class of pārājika offenses, sometimes in the class of saṅghādisesa offenses, sometimes in the class of thullaccaya offenses, sometimes in the class of pācittiya offenses, sometimes in the class of pāṭidesanīya offenses, sometimes in the class of dukkaṭa offenses. Among the six origins of offenses, they arise from six origins: sometimes they arise from the body, not from speech, not from mind; sometimes they arise from speech, not from the body, not from mind; sometimes they arise from the body and from speech, not from mind; sometimes they arise from the body and from mind, not from speech; sometimes they arise from speech and from mind, not from the body; sometimes they arise from the body, from speech, and from mind. Among the four legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. Among the seven principles of settlement, they are settled by three principles of settlement: sometimes by settlement in the presence and by acting according to acknowledgment; sometimes by settlement in the presence and by covering with grass.

Vipattipaccayavāro niṭṭhito catuttho.

The Fourth Section on the Condition of Failure is concluded.

5. Adhikaraṇapaccayavāro

5. 5. The Section on the Condition of a Legal Issue

288. Vivādādhikaraṇapaccayā kati āpattiyo āpajjati? Vivādādhikaraṇapaccayā dve āpattiyo āpajjati – upasampannaṃ omasati, āpatti pācittiyassa; anupasampannaṃ omasati, āpatti dukkaṭassa – vivādādhikaraṇapaccayā imā dve āpattiyo āpajjati.

288. 288. On account of the condition of a legal issue concerning a dispute, how many offenses does one incur? On account of the condition of a legal issue concerning a dispute, one incurs two offenses. If one insults a fully ordained person, it is a pācittiya offense; if one insults a person not fully ordained, it is a dukkaṭa offense. On account of the condition of a legal issue concerning a dispute, one incurs these two offenses.

Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ [T 0.0256] vipattīnaṃ kati vipattiyo bhajanti…pe… sattannaṃ samathānaṃ katihi samathehi sammanti? Tā āpattiyo catunnaṃ vipattīnaṃ ekaṃ vipattiṃ bhajanti – ācāravipattiṃ. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ dvīhi āpattikkhandhehi saṅgahitā – siyā pācittiyāpattikkhandhena, siyā dukkaṭāpattikkhandhena. Channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ tīhi samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhanti – siyā kāyato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti, na vācato; [P 5.0100] siyā vācato ca cittato ca samuṭṭhanti, na kāyato; siyā kāyato ca vācato ca cittato [M 0.0180] ca samuṭṭhanti. Catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ, āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. Sattannaṃ samathānaṃ tīhi samathehi sammanti – siyā sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca, siyā sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca.

Of the four failures, how many failures do those offenses fall under? … By how many of the seven settlements are they settled? Those offenses fall under one of the four failures: failure in conduct. They are included in two of the seven aggregates of offenses: sometimes by the aggregate of pācittiya offenses, sometimes by the aggregate of dukkaṭa offenses. Of the six origins of offenses, they arise from three origins: sometimes they arise from the body and from the mind, not from speech; sometimes they arise from speech and from the mind, not from the body; sometimes they arise from the body, from speech, and from the mind. Of the four legal issues, it is a legal issue concerning an offense. Of the seven settlements, they are settled by three settlements: sometimes by settlement in the presence and by settlement by acknowledgement, sometimes by settlement in the presence and by covering over with grass.
